name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,136

clue.text: Bit of zinc is easily cut into

indicators.note: a bit is only a portion, so the answer is a stretch lifted out of the running letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words once the spaces are ignored

explanation.surface: A metalworker remarks that soft zinc is easy to cut into.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside zINC IS Easily, skipping the first Z and stopping before the rest of 'easily'.
explanation.definitionFit: To incise is to make a cut or engrave a mark into a surface, a precise synonym of carving.

clue.text: Info short on employment for soak

indicators.note: something short is missing its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the word loses its final O
use is employment of something

explanation.surface: Someone is lacking information about a job, phrased like a note to a heavy drinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' just places the second piece after the first in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To infuse tea or herbs is to steep them in liquid, letting them sit and soak.

clue.text: Clash: accord not in it unfortunately

indicators.note: things that go unfortunately go wrong, so the letters end up in a wrong order

blocks.note: thirteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A dispute where, sadly, no agreement has been reached.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is neatly apt: a clash is just what you have when accord is not in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A contradiction is a conflict between statements or facts that cannot both hold, so it is a clash.

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a mitten is a kind of glove

explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken' reads like a lost glove being stolen, but it means charmed, as in 'quite taken with her'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being taken with someone means being attracted to them, the same as being infatuated or lovestruck.

clue.text: Drunk was collared by elderly assassin

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so these letters lurch into another order
a collar goes round a neck, so one piece is ringed by the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
elderly people are old

explanation.surface: An old killer gets arrested while drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Lee Harvey Oswald was the man who shot US President John F. Kennedy in 1963.
explanation.definitionFit: Lee Harvey Oswald is the famous example of an assassin, the gunman who killed President Kennedy.

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: its first letter
a warm person is kind and caring

explanation.surface: A shepherd begins by tending the sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flock' looks like a noun for the sheep, but it is a verb meaning to crowd together.
explanation.definitionFit: People or insects swarm when they move together in a large crowd, just as they flock somewhere.

clue.text: Three stars from Catharine cavorting with Paul

indicators.note: cavorting is leaping about wildly, so the letters jump into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A trio of celebrities emerge from a woman's romp with her partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests film celebrities, but these are real stars in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The nearest star system to our Sun is a triple: Alpha Centauri A and B plus Proxima Centauri.

indicators.note: wrapping goes round a present, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: to see someone is to date them romantically
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to look at the wrapping paper on a present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrapping' and 'gift' both suggest a parcel; 'gift' is actually a verb meaning to give.
explanation.definitionFit: To gift something is to hand it over freely, which is what donating means.

indicators.note: to be outside is to surround, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: a fish is a swimmer
an inn is a small hotel

explanation.surface: A swimmer from Europe stands outside a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' looks like a person, but it is crossword shorthand for a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone or something from Finland is Finnish, and Finland is a country in northern Europe.

indicators.note: something ruined is broken apart, so the letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A cutting piece of writing has spoilt someone's dream.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: a ruined dream is a hard time.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard Times is the Charles Dickens novel satirising the grim industrial towns and utilitarian schooling of Victorian England.

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for area
finished means spent, missing its last letter

explanation.surface: A ski resort's slopes are nearly done for the season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Area' looks like part of the definition but is the opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspen is a famous upmarket ski resort town in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado.

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a spat is a petty quarrel
R is the chess abbreviation for rook

explanation.surface: A fish and a bird are squabbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rook' suggests the black bird, but here it is the chess piece, written R.
explanation.definitionFit: The sprat is a small silvery fish of the herring family, often eaten whole.

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so one piece takes in the others

blocks.note: a rant is a tirade
taken as written
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician launches into a wild, uncontrolled outburst.
explanation.walkthrough: MP, Member of Parliament, is the standard crossword politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Rampant describes something spreading or behaving without any check or control, wildly unchecked.

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for duke
something wobbly is unstable

explanation.surface: An aristocrat is unsteady on his feet in a country town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wobbly' looks like an anagram signal but is a plain synonym. Dunstable is a market town in Bedfordshire, north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Dunstable is an English town that grew up around its historic market at a Roman crossroads.

blocks.note: first meaning: long yellow tropical fruit
second meaning: crazy, as in 'gone bats'

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like the name of the animal, fruit bats; 'bats' is actually slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the plural of a common curved fruit and an informal adjective meaning mad or crazy.

blocks.note: first meaning: cowardly
second meaning: the bright colour of a canary

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as comparing two birds; 'Chicken' is slang for cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is informal for cowardly and is also the colour name for the plumage of the familiar pet songbird.

clue.text: Seneca spoiled attempt to raise spirits

indicators.note: something spoiled has been damaged, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The Roman philosopher Seneca ruined an effort to cheer people up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise spirits' suggests cheering up, but here spirits are ghosts.
explanation.definitionFit: A séance is a meeting where people try to contact and summon the dead.

blocks.note: alimony is paid to a former spouse, an ex
a claim is a demand

explanation.surface: A divorcing spouse is told to state firmly what they want in support payments.
explanation.walkthrough: An alimony demand is an ex's claim, so the pieces go in that order.
explanation.definitionFit: To exclaim is to cry out suddenly and forcefully, voicing words loudly and with feeling.

clue.text: Confuse daughter twice introduced to beer

indicators.note: something introduced to a thing is put into it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: ale is a beer
D for daughter, written twice

explanation.surface: A father befuddles his daughter by giving her beer twice.
explanation.walkthrough: D for daughter is a common abbreviation in family trees.
explanation.definitionFit: To addle someone's brain is to muddle it, leaving them confused and unable to think clearly.

indicators.note: strangely means in an odd way, so the letters come out in an odd order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Part of a bomb is oddly not reacting.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sets an inert part against an explosive one, a neat contrast.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitre, potassium nitrate, is the oxidising ingredient of gunpowder, so it is part of an explosive.

indicators.note: a covering wraps around, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: lard is pig fat
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A wealthy landholder is plump all over.
explanation.walkthrough: A laird is a Scottish word for the owner of a landed estate.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland a laird is the proprietor of a large estate, so a landowner of rank.

blocks.note: surface reading: what a solar-powered cell does
setter's reading: a battering, an assault, from the sun on bare skin

explanation.walkthrough: A battery is also a physical attack, so a solar battery is a beating from the sun, and its effect is painful reddened skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Overexposure to the sun's ultraviolet rays leaves skin red, sore and damaged.

blocks.note: W is an abbreviation for with
Inter Milan is an Italian football club

explanation.surface: A sports fan spends the season following an Italian football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link word but gives its abbreviation W, as in 'w/'.
explanation.definitionFit: Winter is one of the four seasons of the year, the coldest one.

indicators.note: someone high is intoxicated and out of order, so the letters get muddled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Lavish compliments offered in support of Hope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High praise' reads as a single phrase; 'High' is separate, meaning drunk or stoned.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to long or aim for something, the verb sense of wishing and hoping.
